The Mexican flounder (Cyclopsetta chittendeni) is a member of the Paralichthyidae family that inhabits the continental shelf waters of the western Atlantic. Field studies indicate that this species achieves a maximum total length of 32 cm [Li = 32 cm], a value that positions it as a moderately sized flatfish within its genus. Oviparous reproduction occurs through broadcast spawning, where pelagic eggs are released into the water column. The fertilised ova have an egg diameter of approximately 1 mm, and from this dimension the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.000524 grams [Wwb = 0.000524 grams], representing the mass of the chorionate embryo at the moment of gametic union. Under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable thermal regime of 24.8 °C [T = 24.8 °C], zygote formation gives way to a developmental sequence that culminates in larval eclosion after 9 days [ab = 9 days]. This incubation period is consistent with values reported for other warm-water paralichthyids and reflects the rapid embryogenesis permitted by elevated ambient temperatures. The yolk-dependent embryo relies entirely on endogenous reserves until the trophic switch to first exogenous feeding occurs shortly after the mouth gape opens.

Following the transition from the lecithotrophic larva to the actively feeding pelagic larva, individual growth proceeds at a pace shaped by temperature and prey availability. The free-swimming larva experiences a period of rapid mass increase before the onset of larval metamorphosis, during which the morphological transformation toward a benthic habitus occurs. At a constant temperature of 24.8 °C [T = 24.8 °C], individuals reach total length at puberty measured at 17 cm [Lp = 17 cm], signalling the recruitment into the sub-adult population that has achieved gonadal maturation. Body mass at this developmental milestone is 59.8 grams [Wwp = 59.8 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship specific to Cyclopsetta chittendeni. Puberty corresponds to the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, initiating the transition from an immature post-metamorphic stage to a reproductively viable organism. The accumulation of somatic tissue during the juvenile phase is substantial, as individuals more than double their mass in the interval between metamorphic climax and the completion of sexual maturation. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the length at first spawning is tightly linked to habitat quality and local productivity regimes.

As individuals continue to grow beyond the pubertal event, biometric surveys of large specimens reveal that the species achieves a maximum wet weight of 427.5 grams [Wwi = 427.5 grams] at its ultimate total length. This asymptotic mass underscores the energetic ceiling imposed by the demersal foraging strategy typical of the species. The sexually mature adult is iteroparous, engaging in multiple spawning events throughout the reproductive season. When maintained at the species' preferred thermal regime of 24.8 °C [T = 24.8 °C], the maximum reproductive rate has been studied through captive holding experiments. Females produce approximately 210,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 210,000 eggs per year], a figure that represents the highest recorded annual fecundity under optimal conditions. Field observations suggest that actual fecundity varies with female body condition and food availability. The pelagic eggs are transparent and buoyant, drifting with currents until embryogenesis completes and the chorion ruptures to release the yolk-sac larva.

Longevity data for Mexican flounder indicate that the lifespan reaches approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] under natural conditions at 24.8 °C [T = 24.8 °C]. This maximum recorded longevity is modest relative to larger-bodied flatfishes such as Hippoglossus or Paralichthys dentatus, yet it allows for multiple breeding seasons across the adult lifetime. The senescent adult eventually succumbs to natural mortality, with progressive physiological deterioration culminating in organismal death. Field records show that the oldest documented individuals are typically those inhabiting deeper shelf waters where fishing pressure is reduced. The reproductive strategy of broadcast spawning, combined with a moderate maximum age, produces a life-history pattern where early maturation at the pubertal length of 17 cm [Lp = 17 cm] ensures that at least a few spawning seasons occur before senescence sets in. The wet weight at puberty of 59.8 grams [Wwp = 59.8 grams] indicates that maturation coincides with a substantial investment in gonadal tissue relative to somatic mass, a common pattern among iteroparous flatfishes that allocate resources across multiple years.

Ecologically, Cyclopsetta chittendeni occupies a trophic niche as a benthic carnivore, preying on small crustaceans and polychaetes. The pelagic larval phase, during which the planktonic larva feeds on copepod nauplii, lasts until the post-larval transformation triggers benthic settlement. The initial mass of the freshly hatched prolarva, calculated as 0.000524 grams [Wwb = 0.000524 grams], places the species at the small end of the flatfish larval size spectrum, yet rapid growth during the exotrophic phase compensates for this diminutive start. Comparative analysis with sympatric paralichthyids reveals that the ultimate total length of 32 cm [Li = 32 cm] is near the family average for shelf-dwelling species, while the ultimate wet weight of 427.5 grams [Wwi = 427.5 grams] indicates a relatively robust body shape for a fish of that length. The temperature of 24.8 °C [T = 24.8 °C] approximates the mean summer sea surface temperature across much of the species' Gulf of Mexico range, suggesting that the developmental and reproductive metrics are adapted to a warm, stable thermal environment. Age-structured population models incorporate the lifespan of approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] to estimate generation times and inform fisheries management strategies for this commercially harvested species at a temperature of 24.8 °C [T = 24.8 °C].
